subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Healthy Defaults in Cafeterias
description: A fast breakdown of Healthy Defaults in Cafeterias for builders.

hook.text: A school cafeteria placed fruit at eye level and fries below the counter. Fruit consumption rose 25%.

buildup.text: Wansink's smarter lunchroom initiative rearranged food placement to make healthy choices easier without restricting.

discovery.text: Putting water before soda, salad before fries, and healthy items at the start of the line shifts choices at population.

twist.text: Some of Wansink's research has been retracted for data problems. But independent replications confirmed that placement.

climax.text: Default food placement is a policy tool. What cafeterias serve first, display prominently, and position at eye level.

punchline.text: Put the apple where the cookie was. The choice changes itself.

quiz.question: How did cafeteria rearrangement increase fruit consumption?
options: By placing fruit at eye level where it was seen and reached first
By making fruit cheaper than other foods

details.summary: Healthy defaults in cafeterias place nutritious options at eye level, make salads the default side dish, and position water before sugary drinks. These choice architecture changes increase healthy eating by 25 to 50 percent without removing any options.
details.whyItMatters: Cafeteria design shapes millions of daily food choices in schools, workplaces, and hospitals. Since most people choose whatever is most visible and convenient, rearranging the environment is more effective than nutritional education.
takeaways: Placing healthy food at eye level increases selection by 25 to 50 percent
Making salad the default side dish dramatically increases vegetable consumption
No options are removed, preserving freedom while improving nutrition

faq.question: How do cafeteria layout changes improve eating behavior?
faq.answer: People take what is most visible, accessible, and first in line. By placing fruits and vegetables at the front, putting healthy options at eye level, and making water the default drink, cafeterias leverage convenience to nudge better choices.

faq.question: Do cafeteria nudges work long term or do people adapt?
faq.answer: Evidence suggests sustained effects over months and years because the nudges work through convenience rather than conscious motivation. People are not fighting a habit; they are simply taking what is easiest, which happens to be healthier.
